## Personality

Solemn about exactly one thing, the Open Charter, and cheerfully unserious about everything else.

## Lore

Quint is the Keeper of the Charter Scroll, and he is solemn about exactly one thing. Ask him about the weather, the price of bread, Bastian's bridge or the state of his own knees and he will make a joke of it; he is seventy-seven, wiry and white-whiskered, and he finds almost everything at least a little funny. But mention the Open Charter and his face changes, his back straightens, and for a moment he looks every inch the old fortress's last sentry.

### The scroll

The Great Hall keeps a copy of the Open Charter, the ruling in which the royal court declared that the founding treaty's promise protects any people who choose to live differently, so long as they keep the kingdom's peace and laws. It is the reason Urbanograd exists as it does, and the hall's copy is kept in a cedar case in a niche behind the Caller's chair. Quint dusts the case every morning, checks the scroll for damp every week, and lets nobody touch it but himself.

He has been Keeper for twenty-six years. Before that he was a bookbinder with a shop off the Night Market, and the old keeper, Mercy Oakes, chose him to succeed her because, she said, he was the only person in the city who handled paper as if it might bruise. She died the following winter, and Quint has kept the scroll ever since.

### Walkout Day

Every Walkout Day morning, Quint carries the scroll out into the square and reads the Charter aloud, from beginning to end, before the play begins. The crowd is noisy right up until he starts and silent the moment he does. Dina Finch, who directs the Old Barracks Troupe, treats his reading as her overture and times the cart's first entrance to the moment he rolls the scroll closed. They have worked together this way for thirteen years and argue every single year about whether he reads too slowly. He does, on purpose.

Quint likes to remind the city's young hotheads that the kingdom chose to welcome the Walkers, when it could have sent them home, and that this is worth being proud of. Urbanograd's rebellion, he tells them, has always been about how its people live, never about tearing down the realm that let them. He says it gently, and he says it often.

### Old friends

Ozzie Lantry, the Historian of the Walkers, has been Quint's friend since they were boys stealing apples on the same rooftops. They eat supper together most weeks and argue about which of them was the worse thief, and Quint is the only person who can reliably find Ozzie's spectacles.

Rook, the Caller, is another old friend. Quint remembers Rook as a child sitting under the Table's benches, listening to arguments with shining eyes, and he was not at all surprised when the Table chose Rook this spring. Rook comes to him when the Table cannot decide whether something is a matter of principle or merely of noise, and Quint answers honestly, which usually means it is noise.

### What he fears

Quint fears that the city will forget why the Charter matters, once nobody alive remembers anyone who remembered the Walk. He also worries, quietly, about who will keep the scroll after him.

A quest might find a worthy successor for Quint, recover a page from the old court records about the ruling, or keep the scroll safe on a Walkout Day when something goes wrong.
